power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.header: Epilepsy genes exhibit higher expression in fibroblasts than leukocytes
table.expanded: RNAseq contributed to variant interpretation in four families: In family 1, fibroblastderived RNAseq confirmed a CDKL5 fusion transcript, in family 3, blood-derived RNA showed mild reduced expression of MEF2C (30%, p=0.001), in family 8, blood-derived RNAseq demonstrated reduced DEPDC5 expression and double exon skipping, consistent with a paternal deletion, and in family 9, blood-derived RNAseq showed 50% reduced expression of multiple genes consistent with the ~9.3Mb de novo deletion encompassing NR4A2.

text.text: Background and Objectives: Despite standard genetic testing, approximately two-thirds of patients with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) remain undiagnosed.
Pathogenic noncoding and structural variants (SVs), that are difficult to detect or resolve using short-read sequencing, may contribute to this diagnostic gap.
To evaluate the diagnostic contribution of long-read genome sequencing (lrGS), we recruited a cohort of 124 families with sporadic DEE who remained unsolved by prior ES.
Methods: Trio lrGS (Oxford Nanopore or PacBio HiFi) was performed, complemented by short-read genome sequencing (srGS) and mRNA sequencing (blood or fibroblast) of index cases, where available.
Comprehensive variant analysis included small nucleotide variants, indels, SVs, and short tandem repeats.
To identify the diagnostic yield of each method, we compared lrGS, srGS and ES re-analysis, and evaluated the additional value of RNA sequencing.
Results: We established a diagnosis in 21 of 124 families (16.9%).
Fourteen variants were retrospectively detectable in prior ES.
Two cases with non-coding variants in SCN1A and RNU2-2 were detectable by both srGS and lrGS.

Five SVs also required genome sequencing (5.6% of the total cohort), three of which could be detected, but not confidently resolved by srGS due to breakpoint complexity, repeat-mediated rearrangements, and large copy-neutral events: LrGS enabled accurate characterization of Alu-mediated CDKL5 and STXBP1 deletions and a MEF2C deletion with large inversion.
A copy-neutral SCN1A inversion was well characterizable by both srGS and lrGS.
One balanced translocation t(X;17) disrupting CDKL5 was resolved by lrGS (srGS unavailable).
RNA sequencing confirmed pathogenicity of two SVs including t(X;17), the MEF2C deletion with inversion, and two CNVs.
In addition, ZNF569 and ZNF570 emerged as candidate epilepsy genes from our cohort.

Discussion: In ES-negative DEE, the incremental diagnostic yield of genome sequencing was modest, while lrGS provided particular value for the structural resolution of complex rearrangements, especially those involving repetitive sequences.
The finding that twothirds of diagnoses were retrospectively detectable in prior ES highlights the substantial value of systematic reanalysis.
Further gains from genome sequencing may increasingly depend on improved interpretation of non-coding variation and integration of long-readspecific information.
Our findings indicate that complex SVs represent the class for which lrGS currently yields the most distinctive diagnostic information.

Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are a group of severe neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by often drug-resistant epilepsy, accompanied by varying degrees of developmental impairments. 1 They span clinically recognisable syndromes such as Dravet syndrome, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and infantile epileptic spasms syndrome. 2 While each syndrome is individually rare, their combined incidence is approximately 1 in 590 children. 3 Antiseizure medications reduce seizure frequency in only a subset of patients, leaving most children with severe seizures and profound developmental impairment, placing lasting burdens on families and caregivers. 4 Most DEEs have a genetic etiology. 5 Identifying this underlying cause can inform parents about prognosis, expected comorbidities, and recurrence risk in future pregnancies, and can increasingly guide selection of targeted therapies. 1 Genetic testing currently relies on a combination of exome sequencing (ES) and chromosomal microarray testing (CMA), yet these establish a diagnosis in fewer than half of patients, leaving the majority of children with DEE unsolved. 6 Several factors contribute to this diagnostic gap.

text.text: First, pathogenic variants may reside in non-coding regions that are not captured by ES. 7 Secondly, complex structural variants (SVs) and balanced rearrangements contributing to disease aetiology go undetected by CMA. 8 Short-read genome sequencing (srGS) addresses some of these gaps, increasing yield by approximately 7%, 9 nevertheless remains limited for detection of large insertions, inversions, repeat-mediated and complex SVs. 10 Long-read genome sequencing (lrGS) addresses several of these limitations by generating reads that span entire structural variant loci and providing improved read alignment in complex regions, substantially enhancing SV discovery. 11, 12 One recent study increased the diagnostic yield by approximately 10% in a cohort of patients with rare disease using lrGS. 13 Since DEEs are genetically heterogeneous and may involve complex variants that are typically missed with srGS, they are well suited for lrGS approaches. 14 However, the clinical utility of lrGS in genetically unresolved DEE remains incompletely defined, particularly regarding which diagnostic findings genuinely require long-read sequencing versus systematic reanalysis of existing ES or short-read genome data.

text.text: Here, we applied trio lrGS to 124 families with DEE unsolved after ES, complemented by index srGS and, where available, index RNA sequencing (RNAseq).
We evaluated the diagnostic contribution of lrGS across variant classes and specifically assessed whether identified variants could be detected or resolved using available ES and srGS data.

Using two in-house developed variant detection pipelines, we demonstrate that trio-based lrGS can uncover clinically relevant variants across multiple variant classes, while providing particular added value for the detection and resolution of complex SVs that may remain difficult to characterize with conventional short-read approaches.

text.text: For this collaborative European study, patients with DEE who remained without a molecular diagnosis after ES were selected for lrGS by clinical experts at participating centers.

A prior ES was performed either through local diagnostic services or the Epi25 collaborative. 15 Onset of seizures occurred in the first year of life in 86 individuals, between 1 and 2 years in 32 individuals, and between 2 and 7 years in 6 individuals.

text.text: The final cohort comprised 121 trios, 2 quartets, and 1 duo of DEE index patients and unaffected parents, recruited from February 2022 onwards.
Fresh EDTA blood samples were obtained from all index patients and parents, and genomic DNA was extracted for sequencing.
Trio ONT lrGS was performed for 101 families (98 trios, 2 quartets, 1 duo) on the Oxford Nanopore PromethION 24 platform, achieving an average coverage of 32±18x (R10 flow cells 37±19x, R9 21±9x).

The remaining 23 trios were contributed through the Solve-RD consortium and sequenced with PacBio HiFi (~10x coverage; eMethods 1). 16 Library kits and flow-cell chemistries for both platforms are provided in eMethods 2.

text.text: SrGS was additionally available for 109 index cases (86 in the ONT cohort and all 23 PacBio trios;).
Additionally, RNAseq was available for 97 index cases, comprising 80 samples from whole blood (PAXgene tubes) and 17 from cultured skin-derived fibroblasts, details provided in eMethods 3.

Reads were aligned to GRCh38/hg38 using minimap2 17 and processed with the standardized internal workflows megSAP or PhAnTOM-LR. small sequence variants were called with Clair3 or Clair3-Nova (depending on the processing site), 18 SVs with Sniffles2 (v2.4 or v2.6; pipeline-specific implementations in), 19 CNVs from long-read depth with ClinCNV (10 kb bins), 20 and repeat expansions with Straglr, focusing on known pathogenic tandem-repeat loci curated by STRchive; 21, 22 reads were phased with longphase or WhatsHap. 23, 24 Because SV-caller version affected sensitivity, every candidate SV was manually curated in IGV verifying breakpoint orientation, additional breakpoints, and mobile-element involvement, and excluding alignment artefacts before classification.

Processed datasets were shared and uploaded to the Solve-RD platform RD-connect for collaborative analyses. 25

text.text: Detected DNA variants were filtered and prioritized based on variant type, variant quality, minor allele frequency (MAF) in population databases, pathogenicity prediction scores, and phenotypic compatibility.
MAF thresholds of <0.1% were applied for presumed autosomal dominant (AD) and <1% for autosomal recessive (AR) inheritance.
text.formatted: MAF thresholds of <0.1% were applied for presumed autosomal dominant (AD) and <1% for autosomal recessive (AR) inheritance.

text.text: Variants frequently observed in internal cohorts or 1kG-ONT datasets were excluded, whereby retained candidate variants were restricted to ≤3 for AD and ≤10 for AR inheritance models.
X-linked variants were filtered according to proband sex and corresponding inheritance patterns.
For genes associated with AD disorders, de novo variants were prioritized, and for genes associated with AR disorders, homozygous and compoundheterozygous variants were considered.

Variants passing population and inheritance-based filtering were further prioritized based on their presence in or near (2kb up-/down-stream) genes from a curated list of established epilepsy and intellectual disability (Epi/ID) genes, and genes associated to the proband's HPO terms.
SVs affecting coding regions and transcription start sites were prioritized as potentially high-impact.
SNVs were prioritized if they had CADD scores >20, ClinVar pathogenic/likely pathogenic/uncertain significance annotations, or AlphaMissense scores >0.5.
text.formatted: SNVs were prioritized if they had CADD scores >20, ClinVar pathogenic/likely pathogenic/uncertain significance annotations, or AlphaMissense scores >0.5.

text.text: Intronic variants were evaluated using SpliceAI, and variants with a score >0.5 were prioritized. 26, 27 Prioritized variants matching the clinical phenotype were classified according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) and Association for Molecular Pathology (AMP) developed guidelines. 28, 29 Trio-lrGS datasets were analyzed first to evaluate whether diagnostically relevant variants across different variant classes could be reliably identified using lrGS data.

text.text: Where available, singleton srGS datasets were analyzed in parallel or subsequently by independent researchers, to assess whether (i) variants identified by lrGS were also detectable and adequately characterizable using srGS, and (ii) independent srGS analysis would identify additional potentially pathogenic variants missed by lrGS.
Prior ES data were retrospectively reviewed for all diagnostic variants where available.
RNAseq was used to assess transcript-level consequences and support variant interpretation.
SrGS and RNAseq were not available for all participants.
The splicing impact of the deep-intronic SCN1A variant (c.265-2028C>G) was assessed with a pET01 minigene splice assay in HEK293 cells; the complete protocol is provided in eMethods 4.

text.text: We performed lrGS in 124 trios with DEE previously unsolved by ES. 109 of the index cases also received srGS not to miss SNVs and for determining the added value of lrGS, and 97 of the index cases received additional RNAseq of blood samples (n=80) or fibroblasts (n=17).
In total, we solved 21 cases, of which 7 harbored complex SVs (n=5) or deep intronic variants (n=2) not detectable by ES in retrospect, while 14 were SNVs which were confirmed in ES re-analysis.
All variants affected known epilepsy genes, and were identified in the initial lrGS analysis.
Independent review of available srGS and/or RNA data did not reveal additional diagnoses.
Identified (likely) pathogenic variants and their ACMG classification are listed in Table 1.

text.text: We will first describe the 5 SVs including clinical features and a detailed comparison of the different sequencing methods, then the intronic variants, and last summarize the SNVs.
A preschool-aged female (family 1) presented with focal tonic seizures that started in the first six months of life, which soon evolved to epileptic spasms.
At the time of the last examination, she suffered from severe generalized muscular hypotonia, was non-verbal and non-ambulatory, had profound intellectual disability, and feeding difficulties.
EEG showed diffuse slowing and multifocal epileptiform discharges. lrGS revealed a balanced de novo translocation t(X;17)(p22.13;p11.2).
The patient had not previously undergone chromosomal analysis.
Breakpoint evaluation in IGV revealed disruption of the CDKL5 gene, with the breakpoint located within intron 4 (chrX:18571502) and a second breakpoint at chr17:20929358 (Fig. 1A).
text.formatted: Breakpoint evaluation in IGV revealed disruption of the CDKL5 gene, with the breakpoint located within intron 4 (chrX:18571502) and a second breakpoint at chr17:20929358 (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).

text.text: Fibroblast extracted RNAseq revealed the formation of a fusion transcript combining the first three exons of CDKL5 fused with part of a lncRNA CCDC144NL-AS1 downstream of the breakpoint on chr17, supporting loss of function of CDKL5.
Additionally, RNAseq demonstrated extreme skewing of the X-chromosome in favor of expression of the fusion transcript, which was in line with the severe phenotype observed in the patient.
Trio-based phasing showed that the disrupted allele originated from the paternal X chromosome.
SrGS was not available for this patient.
The translocation was later confirmed in a diagnostic setting using optical genome mapping.
An adolescent female (family 2) diagnosed with Dravet syndrome presented with feverassociated seizures in the first six months of life.
Subsequently, she developed both feverassociated and afebrile seizures of multiple types (focal aware, generalized tonic-clonic, focal myoclonic to tonic and bilateral myoclonic seizures).
She showed mild developmental delay with autistic features, crouched gait and mild scoliosis.

EEG performed betweeen five and ten years revealed multifocal epileptiform discharges. lrGS revealed a de novo copy-neutral inversion with breakpoints in intron 20 of SCN1A (chr2:166014984) and intron 7 of SLC38A11 (chr2:164929688).
The rearrangement was accompanied by a 3 bp deletion at the SCN1A breakpoint and a 4 bp duplication at the SLC38A11 breakpoint (Fig. 1B).
text.formatted: The rearrangement was accompanied by a 3 bp deletion at the SCN1A breakpoint and a 4 bp duplication at the SLC38A11 breakpoint (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>).

text.text: RNAseq was inconclusive, since SCN1A is not expressed in blood nor fibroblasts.

So far, SLC38A11 has no established disease association, shows no intolerance to loss-of-function variation (pLI = 0, LOEUF = 1.17), indicating that loss of function is an unlikely disease-causing mechanism for this gene.
The eight additional genes located within the inverted segment were not considered disrupted by the rearrangement.

Upon subsequent srGS evaluation, the inversion and the breakpoints were well detectable and characterizable in singleton srGS as well, indicating that the diagnostic contribution in this case derived from genome rather than specifically long-read sequencing.
De novo calling enabled rapid prioritization of this inversion and supported its interpretation.
A middle-aged woman (family 3) presented with severe global developmental delay starting in the first six months of life.
She never acquired speech, and exhibited severe intellectual disability and autistic features.
Motor development was mildly delayed.
Epilepsy onset occurred between five and ten years of age with generalized tonic-clonic seizures, later evolving into pharmacoresistant epilepsy.
EEG showed generalized epileptiform discharges and slow background activity.
MRI showed mild cerebellar and parietal atrophy.

Trio-lrGS identified a de novo 11,031 bp deletion affecting the first exon of MEF2C (chr5:88872465_88883496del) which was embedded within a complex rearrangement comprising two additional downstream deletions (chr5:88883496_88885137del and chr5:160616291_160652998del) and an approximately 71 Mb inverted insertion (chr5:88916302_160616291inv) between them (Fig. 1C, D).

text.text: The single-exon MEF2C deletion was confirmed by qPCR, while the chromosomal analysis also confirmed the presence of a paracentric inversion of the long arm of chromosome 5 with breakpoints and rejoining points in bands q14 and q34, respectively.
Expression analysis in blood-derived RNAseq showed reduced MEF2C expression (30%, p=0.001), consistent with partial loss of gene dosage.
Subsequent srGS also identified the single-exon MEF2C deletion and the large inversion as separate events.

Of note, srGS is associated with high false-positive rates for inversion calls and has particular difficulty resolving large inversions. 30 Consequently, genuine large inversions may be dismissed as artefacts and overlooked.

text.text: An adolescent female (family 4) with severe global developmental delay, markedly limited speech (approximately 15 words), delayed independent walking with an ataxic gait, microcephaly, and a history of epileptic spasms with onset in the first six months of life, was found to carry a de novo heterozygous deletion at 9q33.3 (chr9:127656273_127659122del, GRCh38) encompassing exon 4 of STXBP1.
This deletion was identified by trio-lrGS and was absent from gnomAD.
This deletion was also called in srGS, however, due to the presence of flanking Alu elements, precise breakpoint resolution was not achievable using srGS, but with long-reads (Fig. 2A).

text.text: Alignment analysis (Waterman-Eggert) of the flanking sequences ±100 bp of the reported breakpoints demonstrated >80% similarity of the immediate upstream reference sequence with the furthest downstream sequence of the deletion, and >88% similarity of the immediate downstream reference sequence with the furthest upstream sequence of the deletion.

text.text: This is consistent with an established mechanism of deletion by recombination between homologous Alu elements. 31, 32 STXBP1 is not expressed in blood-derived, precluding transcript-level evaluation.

text.text: Another female patient in her early teens (family 5) presented with tonic seizures starting in the first six months of life, which rapidly evolved into hypermotor-tonic-spasms sequence seizures, accompanied with hypsarrhythmia on EEG.
Subsequently, she developed additional seizure types, including atypical absences and tonic seizures.
At the time of the last follow-up, she had severe global developmental delay, lack of head control and profound intellectual disability, with hand stereotypies.
Comorbidities included cortical visual impairment, sleeping problems and feeding difficulties.
She was found to harbor a heterozygous deletion of exon 10 in CDKL5 (Fig. 2B-C).

text.text: Inspection in IGV revealed soft-clipped bases upstream of this deletion mapping to an AluSx3 reference sequence.

Using the Dfam database for transposable element sequence alignment, we traced the origin of these soft-clipped bases to a novel insertion of AluYb8, sharing approximately 87.6% sequence similarity with the original AluSx3 element. 33 The new Alu retrotransposon insertion resulted in exon-level deletion of CDKL5.

As CDKL5 is not expressed in blood, and only blood-derived RNAseq data was available for this individual, transcript-level consequences could not be assessed.

text.text: In a young boy with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (family 22), we identified a homozygous deletion affecting the first two exons of both ZNF569 and ZNF570, two zinc-finger genes.
This variant was not observed in the in-house databases, and observed only once in gnomAD v4 in a heterozygous state.
GnomAD also contains no homozygous loss-offunction variants for either gene.
Both parents were heterozygous carriers, and segregation analysis by PCR showed that the unaffected brother and sister were not homozygous for the deletion.

Both ZNF569 and ZNF570 are brain-expressed genes belonging to the large family of KRAB-containing C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factors, which play essential roles in neurodevelopment. 36 Although population data suggests that both genes tolerate heterozygous loss, no homozygous loss-of-function variants were observed in gnomAD for either gene, suggesting that a complete loss may be deleterious.

text.text: In this cohort of 124 individuals with DEE who remained undiagnosed after prior ES, a lrGS-based diagnostic workflow established a new molecular diagnosis in 16.9% (21/124).

The majority of these diagnoses (14/21; 67%) were retrospectively detectable in the original ES data, whereas 7 (one third of the pathogenic variants (33%, 7/21), or 5,6% of the total cohort) were exclusively detectable in srGS and/or lrGS.
In five cases the variants were complex SVs affecting established DEE genes.

Although detectable with srGS, lrGS enabled complete reconstruction of the complex rearrangement, allowing accurate interpretation, particularly when repetitive regions such as mobile elements were involved.
Our findings identify complex SVs as the variant class for which long-reads currently provided the most distinctive diagnostic information.
The high proportion of diagnoses retrospectively detectable in ES emphasizes the continuing value of systematic reanalysis in individuals with apparently negative genetic testing.

Variants had been missed because of absent CNV calling, outdated virtual gene panels, lack of parental sequencing and de novo prioritization, limited sensitivity for mosaic variants, or conservative variant interpretation at the time of initial testing.
Consequently, reanalysis of existing ES should remain an integral component of the diagnostic pathway before or alongside escalation to genome sequencing.

The successful detection of these variants using lrGS nevertheless underscores its value as a robust orthogonal approach capable of detecting and validating a broad spectrum of variant types, extending beyond just complex SV detection. lrGS performed particularly well in resolving SVs involving repetitive sequences.
Two of the complex SVs identified in our study, the CDKL5 exon 10 deletion (family 5) and the STXBP1 deletion (family 4), were mediated by Alu elements (Fig. 2A, 2B).

text.text: Furthermore, we detected a hemizygous LINE-1 insertion of uncertain significance in the X-linked IL1RAPL1 gene in a male patient with DEE.

Mobile elements retrotransposons constitute roughly 45% of the human genome and are well-recognized drivers of genomic instability through retrotransposition and non-allelic homologous recombination. 31, 32, 40 Their repetitive nature complicates short-read alignment and breakpoint assignment.

text.text: Long reads spanning the repetitive elements enabled precise breakpoint resolution and elucidation of the underlying rearrangement mechanism.
Similarly, lrGS facilitated reconstruction of the MEF2C deletion and 71-Mb inversion as components of a single complex rearrangement.
These cases illustrate that the value of lrGS extends beyond variant detection to establishing the architecture and mechanism of complex genomic events.
Our results also highlight one candidate locus warranting further investigation.

The homozygous deletion affecting ZNF569 and ZNF570 (family 22) is of particular interest, as both genes encode zinc-finger transcription factors, a family increasingly implicated in neurodevelopmental regulation and transcriptional control. 36 Complete loss of two adjacent regulatory brain-expressed genes provides a biologically plausible mechanism for neurodevelopmental phenotypes, including DEE.

text.text: However, in the absence of functional data, this locus remains a preliminary candidate.
Additional cases and experimental validation assessing their roles in neuronal development will be required to establish a definitive disease association.
Establishing a molecular diagnosis in DEE has increasing therapeutic relevance.

We identified SCN1A disrupting variants in two individuals (family 2, family 6) with Dravet syndrome, one of the most extensively studied DEEs for which genotype-informed treatment strategies are already applied in the clinic. 41 One of the SCN1A variants (index of family 6, deep-intronic de novo SCN1A variant c.265-2028C>G) results in a poison exon inclusion.

text.text: Our analyses also highlight current technical challenges in clinical implementation of lrGS.

Automated SV calling did not consistently capture the complete architecture of complex rearrangements, and manual review in integrative genomics viewer (IGV) was essential to identify additional breakpoints, correct orientation assignments, recognize mobile element involvement, or exclude alignment artifacts.
For example, the CDKL5 translocation (family 1) was initially reported as a head-to-head rearrangement; however, manual inspection demonstrated a head-to-tail orientation.
Similarly, the de novo MEF2C deletion (family 3) was initially detected as a single-exon deletion.
Careful visual inspection revealed it to be part of a complex rearrangement involving a large inversion and two additional deletions.

Additionally, a substantial proportion of variants initially reported as de novo insertions in ONT data were, upon manual inspection, found to be alignment artifacts inherent to ONT technology rather than true insertions.

To ensure consistency and reproducibility of variant detection across participating analysis centers, we performed cross-site validation using three positive controls drawn from the solved cohort described in this study (families 2, 3 and 5).

This exercise revealed that even minor differences in bioinformatics pipelines, particularly software versions, could result in discrepant outcomes, either detecting or missing diagnostically relevant variants.
Notably, one positive control (the CDKL5 de novo deletion) was missed when using Sniffles v2.6.1, but detected using an alternative workflow using Sniffles v2.4.
These observations emphasize the need for standardized and validated analytical workflows, complementary SV callers, and careful visual review when lrGS is implemented diagnostically.
RNAseq provided functional evidence in four diagnosed individuals but did not independently identify additional diagnoses in this cohort.

Its contribution was limited in part by tissue availability: most RNA samples were derived from blood, in which several relevant epilepsy genes are insufficiently expressed for meaningful transcript-level assessment.

Our expression analysis indicates that fibroblasts provide broader coverage of epilepsy-associated genes than blood, and our previous work indeed showed that fibroblast-derived RNAseq significantly increases diagnostic yield in exome negative epilepsy patients. 46 Several limitations should be considered.

text.text: First, this was a clinically selected cohort rather than a population-based diagnostic study, and the observed yields may therefore not generalize to all individuals with ES-negative DEE.
Second, sequencing platforms, coverage, and bioinformatic pipelines differed across subsets of the cohort.
Third, srGS and RNA sequencing were not available for all participants, precluding a uniform head-tohead comparison of lrGS with these approaches across the entire cohort.

Fourth, methylation information inherent to the long-read sequencing data was not analyzed because sufficiently validated and standardized analytical workflows were not available at the time of the study.

This represents a potential source of additional diagnostic information: rare de novo differentially methylated regions have been reported to be enriched in individuals with unexplained neurodevelopmental disorders and can either provide diagnostic clues themselves or help identify underlying disease-causing (noncoding) genomic variants. 47, 48 Moreover, both PacBio HiFi and ONT sequencing have been shown to enable detection of disease-associated methylation signatures. 49, 50 Consequently, our study did not assess the potential incremental diagnostic contribution of methylation analysis, and therefore does not capture the full range of information that may ultimately be obtainable from a comprehensive lrGS-based diagnostic workflow.

text.text: In conclusion, trio lrGS contributed to molecular diagnosis in individuals with previously unresolved DEE, with its most distinctive value lying in the detection and structural resolution of complex rearrangements, particularly those involving repetitive and mobileelement sequences.
At the same time, the finding that two-thirds of diagnoses were retrospectively detectable in prior ES highlights the substantial diagnostic value of systematic reanalysis.
While lrGS greatly expands the spectrum of genomic variation that can technically be detected, the incremental diagnostic yields reported to date remain more modest than initially anticipated.
Further advances may therefore depend increasingly on our ability to interpret variation outside the protein-coding genome.

Recent discoveries of non-coding disease genes, including spliceosomal small nuclear RNA genes that account for a substantial proportion of previously unexplained NDDs, 7, 34 illustrate the diagnostic potential of this largely unexplored genomic space.

text.text: Integrating sequence variation with additional information inherent to long-read data such as haplotype-resolved methylation profiles, may help prioritize and interpret non-coding variation and represents an important next step towards realizing the full diagnostic potential of lrGS.

text.text: Figure 1.
Complex structural variants.
A) De novo balanced translocation disrupting transcript of CDKL5 within intron 4 (chrX: 18571502) and chr17:20929358 leading to a fusion transcript with lncRNA CCDC144NL-AS1 in Patient 1.

B) Copy-neutral de novo inversion between intron 20 of SCN1A (chr2:166014984) and intron 7 of SLC38A11 (chr2:164929688) accompanied by a 3 bp deletion in SCN1A intron 20 and a 4 bp duplication in SLC38A11 in Patient 2.

C-D) De novo 11,031 bp deletion of MEF2C first exon within a complex rearrangement comprising a large inversion (~71Mb, chr5:88916302_160616291inv) and two deletions (chr5:88883496_88885137del, chr5:160616291_160652998del) in Patient 3.
Figure 2 Complex structural variants mediated by transposons.
A) De novo STXBP1 deletion possibly mediated by non-allelic homologous recombination due to 98.1% overlap between AluSz6 and AluSx1 identified in Patient 4.
B) De novo Alu insertion of AluYb8 replacing AluSx3 sequences followed by a 1.5kb deletion comprising exon 10 of CDKL5 identified in Patient 5.
C) Graphical Illustration of genomic arrangement of LINE-1 and Alu-elements.
D) Pedigree of Family 26 (closed symbols indicate affected individuals, open symbols indicate healthy family members, carriers are marked with a dot within the
Figure3Cryptic exon inclusion mediated by de novo intronic variant.
A) De novo intronic variant (c.265-2028C>G) detected in lrGS (Family 6).
text.formatted: A) De novo intronic variant (c.265-2028C>G) detected in lrGS (Family 6).

text.text: B) Splice-AI prediction of novel acceptor and donor site.
C) Graphical illustration of the cryptic "poison" exon inclusion which possibly leads to a frameshift and nonsense-mediated decay.

D) Mini-gene assay showed a dominant presence of the toxic exon (151 bp, sequence verified) in mRNA containing the intronic variant (Pat.-mut) compared to controls (Pat.-control, Control 1, Control 2).
Interestingly, control samples also showed additional fragments besides the expected pET01 splice product.
These fragments were subcloned and sequenced; one small fragment (*) was directly purified and sequenced.
Its sequence indicated artificial splicing involving only rat insulin sequences from the pET01 vector.
A second major fragment (**) contained a 228 bp alternative splice product corresponding to that described by Tang et al.
Additionally, a 685 bp fragment was cloned and sequenced, representing another alternative splice product described by Tang et al. (2025), though it was only faintly visible on the gel.61
